title: Portland's Broadway Bridge lifts on pivots that slide away from the river

cover.alt: Two red steel truss leaves of a drawbridge tilted up into a cloudy sky above a river, on concrete piers.

body: The leaf of a drawbridge, or **bascule bridge**, usually pivots on a fixed axle or rocks back on a curved track, with a counterweight balancing it. Portland's Broadway Bridge, opened in 1913 over the Willamette River, uses the rarer [Rall design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bascule_bridge#Types): the pivot is part of the leaf and travels horizontally along a track, away from the channel, while a strut tied to the fixed structure forces the leaf to tip up as it goes. Designed by Ralph Modjeski for $1.6 million, it was the world's longest double-leaf bascule bridge of any type when it opened, and it is still the longest of the Rall type.

slides.heading: Three ways to lift a bascule
items: Fixed trunnion: the leaf pivots on a big axle
Rolling lift: it rocks back on a curved track
Rall: its pivot slides back as a strut tips it up

slides.label: times a month, on average, the draw span opens
slides.text: Meanwhile its four lanes carried about 30,000 vehicles a day in 2006, and streetcars have crossed it again since 2012.

slides.prompt: Why did Portland pick the rare Rall design over its rivals in 1913?
slides.detail: The Strauss, Scherzer and Rall patent holders competed for what was expected to be the world's longest bascule bridge. Rall won on cost.

slides.heading: A century of opening
slides.note: The bridge was black until 1963, when it was repainted 'Golden Gate' red

slides.question: In a Rall bascule, what makes the leaf tip up?
options: A cable winch on a tower
A strut, as the pivot slides back
A gear on a fixed axle
slides.explanation: The pivot travels along a track while a strut linked to the fixed structure turns that sliding into rotation. Broadway is driven through that link.
